title: Memory management
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Could the worst thing that happened to you become your strength?

Jose asked: could every negative thing that has happened to you empower you? A student said: you can learn from it, and the example of someone who sees a harmful home life and decides not to repeat it.

Jose said that some people come from very negative backgrounds and it empowers them: they break the generational cycle. He said the habit did not start with the physical act, it started with the mental act, so how do we catch it?
A student said: you also have to take yourself out of negative environments, and control your path. You do take with you some of the ingrained upbringing, and you are a work in progress.

Jose said that you have to manage your memories: am I remembering this in a way that is productive to me today? He said the productive way to keep a painful memory is to understand why the person acted as they did. Otherwise the memory becomes an anchor and a trigger.

A student said: I have worked for bad managers. I look at what they did wrong and run a mental scenario of how I would have handled it, so I learn from other people's mistakes and from how those mistakes affected me.
What memory could you keep in a more useful way?
Education, not advice. If this is heavy for you, a trained person can help.

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write a hard thing that happened to you.
Write the memory you want to keep in a more useful way.
Write what you learned from a bad manager or example.
Write who you could talk to if it is heavy.

check.q: What did Jose say you have to manage?
What did a student say you also have to do with negative environments?
What can an unmanaged memory become, according to Jose?

recap: Learn from the negative. Manage your memories. Take yourself out of harmful places.
